OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: geopolitical and war news with no resource-economy connection; consumer tech and gadget reviews; wildlife content with no agricultural or working-lands relevance; crime and judicial news unrelated to resource industries; financial market and stock ticker stories.

items.title: [Fast Company] The Amazon rainforest, long known as the ‘lungs of our planet,’ now releases more carbon than it absorbs
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The Amazon rainforest has long been called the “lungs of our planet,” because of how it takes in and stores billions of tons of carbon dioxide. 

But the Amazon has been losing that ability. Years of deforestation, drought, and fires have hindered just how much CO2 the rainforest can absorb. 

Now, the Amazon rainforest often releases more carbon than it takes in, a new study finds. It’s only in the “wettest years” that the rainforest is nearly carbon neutral.

The study, published in the journal Nature, was led by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research and included an international team of researchers. They used 15 years of atmospheric carbon measurements, which had been collected by research planes.

Those years were then grouped by different characteristics, like the level of human activities—which includes deforestation, logging, or using fires to clear land—and the amount of climate stress—like drought or heat waves. 

What the research found

Some years were wet with low human activity, some had low climatic stress but high human activity, and others had “intense global climate events, such as El Niño” along with intense amounts of human activity. 

In the years where the rainforest stayed relatively wet, and where there was relatively low deforestation and few wildfires, the Amazon was nearly carbon neutral. The forest was still a slight source of carbon into the atmosphere, but it “did not significantly contribute to the global carbon balance” in those years, the researchers write.

When drought or heat were mild but deforestation and wildfires occurred more, the net carbon emissions from the Amazon “jumped dramatically,” according to a statement. 

The years with lots of climate stress coupled with lots of damaging human activity were the worst. But they were still close to the net emissions from the second group, which led researchers to say that most of the carbon emitted by the Amazon comes from human activities, predominantly land-use change.

“Global climate and climate-mediated stressors are important modulating factors, but people’s choices about how to use and live on the land surface in this region are key to understanding the movement of carbon between the land and the atmosphere,” says coauthor Jen Johnson, assistant professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Kansas, in a statement. 

This isn’t the first paper to point out that the Amazon is not the grand carbon sink it once was. A 2021 study looked at how, as huge areas of the forest are cut down or burned, its ability to capture carbon was shrinking. 

In 2023, a year of extreme drought and high temperatures, researchers showed how the Amazon became a source of carbon emissions, releasing between 10 and 170 million tons of carbon instead of absorbing it. 

Slow burn

We’ve also long known that human activity is threatening the Amazon’s survival. In 2019, there were more than 74,000 fires burning in Brazil, mostly in the Amazon—80% more than the year before.

And though we often think of these as “wildfires,” they’re primarily set by ranchers who are clearing land for cattle to meet the demand for beef.  

The more deforestation, we know, the drier the Amazon becomes, which makes it even more difficult for the remaining parts of the forest to recover. 

“For many decades, there has been concern about the idea of a tipping point, where gradual drying and gradual loss of the forest could feed back on itself in a self-reinforcing way,” Johnson said.

“That could create a transition from an ecosystem type that has stored huge amounts of carbon in living vegetation to drier forests or other ecosystem types that do not store nearly as much carbon,” she continued. “The more carbon from the Amazon that moves into the atmosphere and stays there, the more trouble our climate system is in.”

Though the outlook is dire if these activities continue, the researchers say that policy changes can help. 

“There’s a clear, policy-relevant prescription that comes from this analysis,” Johnson said. “Measures to bring deforestation down to zero are required to manage net carbon emissions from the Amazon . . . It’s not something that’s out of our control because it’s being driven by global climatic factors—it’s something very much under the control of governments and individuals.”

European Union agriculture ministers agreed on a partial negotiating position for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) after 2027, covering some rules for 2028–2034 but leaving financing and other cross-cutting provisions unresolved. The agreement is not final: negotiations with the European Parliament remain, and the new policy is scheduled to take effect on Jan. 1, 2028. Copa-Cogeca, which represents EU farmers and agricultural cooperatives, warned that the European Commission’s budget proposal could mean cuts of more than 20% in most member states. That estimate is not an adopted EU decision. Poland is pressing for a definition of “active farmer” that directs aid to people who farm without excluding those who also work outside agriculture, and for more flexible environmental requirements.

items.title: [agrapress.it] EU farm deal mandates young-farmer aid, leaves payment caps unresolved
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

European Union agriculture ministers agreed on a partial framework for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) after 2027, requiring countries to increase support for young farmers and develop succession strategies while giving national governments more leeway over implementation. The Council of the EU’s position also strengthens farm risk and crisis management tools, including support for insurance and emergency payments after disasters, animal or plant disease outbreaks, and market disruption. The agreement leaves payment ceilings and reductions for larger land-based subsidies unresolved. Countries will define “active farmer” within a required national framework intended to direct payments toward people doing agricultural work. A proposed redistributive payment would be optional for member states, while common environmental conditions remain alongside incentives that governments can tailor to local farming systems. The Council’s position provides a basis for negotiations with the European Parliament, whose position is expected in 2027. The final rules will also depend on EU budget negotiations. Farmers’ groups and lawmakers are already disputing how much flexibility the deal gives governments and whether its environmental and worker protections are strong enough.

items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

The plaintiffs cite personal harm from heat, wildfire smoke and extreme weather. Canada has warmed about twice as fast as the global average since 1970 and could warm 5 C by century’s end under current global policies, according to federal climate assessments cited in Canadian reporting. Plaintiffs describe smoke-related illness, displacement, flooding and drought. Witnesses are expected to testify over four to five weeks; closing arguments are scheduled for February 2027, with a decision expected later that year.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN urges steep fossil-fuel cuts as 1.5°C overshoot becomes unavoidable
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap Report says governments must now limit the scale and duration of global warming beyond 1.5°C, rather than try to prevent that threshold from being crossed. Its lowest-overshoot pathway would cap warming at 1.7°C to 1.8°C around mid-century, with about a 50% chance of returning to 1.5°C by 2100. Following that pathway requires greenhouse-gas emissions to fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025. The report says existing national climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5% to 8% by 2030 and 11% to 15% by 2035. If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; full delivery of pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. The pathway also calls for sharply reducing coal-fired electricity generation and scaling up carbon removal. The report warns that the required reductions are far beyond current plans. Governments are due to discuss climate action at the COP31 summit, scheduled to open in Antalya on Nov. 9.

The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

In Nevada, self-driving vehicles, casino robots and digital guest services are changing work on the Las Vegas Strip as thousands of tradespeople build data centers near Reno. Analysts and researchers warn that companies may reduce junior hiring because AI handles basic tasks that traditionally helped new workers gain experience. A survey cited by MIT Technology Review Insights found 16% of respondents saw transformative value from AI, while 12% had agents in production. U.S. federal AI regulation remains stalled in Congress, but a local report said the next Congress could take it up in January. items.title: [koaa.com] U.S. emissions rise worsens global warming outlook, UN report says
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 emissions assessment says U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 133 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2025, the largest increase among major economies. The United States accounted for about 70% of the net increase among 124 countries whose emissions grew. The report warns that the world can no longer avoid exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C threshold and must limit the overshoot. The U.S. increase reflected higher electricity demand and a rebound in coal-fired power generation, while global greenhouse-gas emissions remained roughly level at 58.4 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. The assessment attributes its worsening projections partly to the United States’ formal withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions. Under existing policies, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; fully meeting national climate pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. UNEP says a pathway offering about a 50% chance of limiting peak warming to 1.7–1.8°C and returning to 1.5°C by 2100 requires global emissions cuts of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025. The next UN climate summit, COP31, is scheduled to open in Antalya, Türkiye, next month.

items.title: [thehindu.com] Russia and Ukraine agree to Oleshky truce for aid and evacuations
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Russia and Ukraine have agreed to pause fighting around Russian-occupied Oleshky in southern Ukraine to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations under an arrangement brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, officials said Friday. Russia’s military chief and Ukraine’s General Staff said their forces would stop firing at 4 a.m. Moscow time on Oct. 27. The White House had announced Oct. 29 as the ceasefire’s start date, while Ukrainian negotiator Dmytro Lubinets, the country’s human rights ombudsman, said the humanitarian mission would begin on Oct. 29 and the pause would last several days. Oleshky’s population has fallen from about 24,000 before the invasion to an estimated 1,700-2,000, including about 50 children. Residents face shortages of food, medicine and clean water, limited electricity, mined roads and continuing military attacks. The first steps are expected to include assessing residents’ needs and clearing mines before aid convoys enter. Civilian teams are to coordinate transport for those choosing to leave for either Russia or Ukraine. The ceasefire is expected to cover the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation. Lubinets said it would last several days; officials have not provided details on how compliance will be monitored. Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said technical-level talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States are planned for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi.

items.title: [sci.news] Cambridge study finds comets rarely delivered life’s ingredients to Earth
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

A University of Cambridge-led study finds it was extremely unlikely that comets delivered enough hydrogen cyanide, a chemical used in proposed pathways to life, to early Earth. The study, published in Scientific Reports on Oct. 28, used computer simulations to model comet evolution, atmospheric entry and impacts. The team says most impacts would destroy the molecule or fail to leave it at a useful concentration. Of the researchers’ 100,000 simulated histories, 54% included no comet impact that delivered hydrogen cyanide at concentrations considered sufficient for prebiotic chemistry. Comet delivery was more likely on Mars, where lower gravity and a thinner atmosphere make successful impacts more feasible, but the study does not establish that it happened there. The authors point to asteroid impacts or chemical processes on Earth as alternatives; outside researchers say the findings test a specific delivery pathway, not every possible comet contribution.
